opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a pretty varied group, and it's changed a lot over time. In the early days, for things like the InstructGPT work, we were mostly working with contractors through vendors. People with decent writing ability and good judgment, who could read a prompt, look at a few model outputs, and say which one was better and why. A lot of the early effort was simply figuring out how to communicate what we wanted, writing detailed guidelines and iterating on them when we saw disagreements.

As the models got better, the bar for the people rating them went up. If the model is writing reasonably good code or explaining a subtle point in chemistry, you need someone who can tell whether it's actually right, not just whether it sounds fluent. So we've moved more toward people with real domain expertise: programmers, people with STEM backgrounds, people who are careful readers and can catch subtle errors. There's also a big premium on conscientiousness, people who will check the answer instead of going with their first impression.

I'd say the most important qualities are careful judgment and the ability to apply a fairly nuanced spec consistently. Raw expertise matters, but so does taste: noticing when an answer is technically correct but unhelpful, or verbose, or hedging too much. And we're increasingly thinking of it as a collaboration between the human and the model, where raters use AI assistance to evaluate outputs that would be too hard or time-consuming to check unaided. That's going to become more important as the models get stronger, because human judgment alone won't scale to everything we want to supervise.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's a pretty varied group, and it's changed a lot over time. In the early days of RLHF, when we were doing the summarization work and then the first InstructGPT stuff, we were mostly working with contractors who were doing fairly generalist tasks—reading a couple of outputs, picking which one was better, flagging things that were obviously wrong or harmful. And for that kind of work you want people who are careful, who have good judgment, and who can follow a fairly detailed set of guidelines consistently. A lot of them had backgrounds in writing or editing or education, that sort of thing.

But as the models got better, the bottleneck shifted. If the model is already writing pretty competent English and getting basic facts right, then the labeler needs to be able to notice the subtler problems—is this proof actually correct, is this code going to run, is this medical advice something a doctor would sign off on. So increasingly we've been hiring people with real domain expertise. People who've written a lot of code, people with graduate training in math or science, lawyers, people with medical backgrounds. You basically need labelers who are at least as good as the model at the thing you're trying to improve, or you can't get a clean signal.

The other thing I'd say is that the most important quality isn't really raw expertise, it's a kind of conscientiousness. The outputs that cause trouble are often ones that look fine on the surface, and the difference between a good labeler and a mediocre one is whether they actually check rather than skim. We spend a lot of effort on calibration—having multiple people rate the same thing, looking at agreement rates, writing up detailed guidelines and iterating on them when we find disagreements. So it's as much about building a process that produces consistent judgments as it is about the individuals.

And honestly, we've also started leaning on the models themselves to assist with this. Not to replace human judgment, but to help a human labeler find the spot in a long response where something might be wrong. That lets you use expert time more efficiently, which matters because expert time is the scarce resource.
